title: India Sent a Delegation to Russia Last Month. It Came Back Talking About Coal Mines.
excerpt: SAIL and NMDC are exploring acquisitions of coking coal assets in Russia and boosting nickel imports — a quiet but significant pivot in India's raw materials strategy.
body:
India's two largest state-owned mining and steel companies have been quietly talking to Russia about buying coking coal assets and ramping up nickel imports, three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Steel Authority of India (SAIL) and NMDC Ltd sent a delegation to Russia last month for preliminary talks with government and industry executives. SAIL has set up an internal panel to study the issue. The talks are confidential, but the strategic logic is not.

## The Coking Coal Problem

India is the world's second-largest crude steel producer after China. Its blast furnaces — which account for roughly 70% of domestic steel output — run on coking coal, and the country imports most of what it needs. In January, the government designated coking coal a "critical and strategic mineral" on the grounds of import dependence.

Australia has been the traditional supplier, but prices for premium hard coking coal have climbed sharply as some Australian mines suspended operations. Russia, which offered significant discounts during the early phase of Western sanctions, has become an increasingly attractive alternative.

SAIL's chairman, Amarendu Prakash, has previously acknowledged that Russian coking coal has been "much cheaper than coal imports from other countries." The company has been importing roughly 300,000 tonnes per quarter from Russia and now appears ready to move from buying to owning.

## The Nickel Play

Separately, India and Russia held initial talks in New Delhi in April about boosting nickel supplies. India currently imports nickel from China, Japan, Norway, and the United States, with only tiny quantities from Russia — despite Russia being one of the world's largest nickel producers through Nornickel.

The interest is driven by India's electric vehicle ambitions. New Delhi aims for electric vehicles to account for 30% of cars and 80% of two-wheelers by 2030, up from about 6% and 9% now. Nickel is essential for the high-density lithium-ion batteries that power EVs, and securing a stable supply chain is a strategic imperative.

## The Geopolitical Context

The outreach to Russia sits at the intersection of economic necessity and geopolitical calculation. India has maintained a notably independent stance since the Ukraine war began in 2022, refusing to condemn Russia and sharply increasing oil imports at discounted prices. The mineral talks extend that pragmatism into a new domain.

For the Indian diaspora in Western capitals — particularly in the US, UK, and Canada — these deals carry diplomatic freight. Every Indian state-owned acquisition of Russian assets risks friction with Washington, which has pushed allies to reduce economic engagement with Moscow. India's argument has consistently been that its energy and raw material needs are non-negotiable.

The government also wants to secure supplies of lithium, cobalt, and rare earths — minerals that will define the next industrial cycle. The International Coal Ventures Private Limited (ICVL), a joint venture between Indian PSUs, is already looking to double the capacity of its Benga coal mine in Mozambique to 4 million tonnes per annum.

## What Comes Next

Neither SAIL, NMDC, nor India's steel ministry responded to Reuters' requests for comment. Russia's energy ministry also declined to respond. The silence is telling — these are early-stage talks, not done deals.

But the direction of travel is clear. India is building a multi-continent sourcing strategy for the raw materials its steel mills and EV factories need, and Russia is firmly on the map. Whether Washington objects is a question New Delhi appears prepared to answer later.
